idiom_name: value-returning functions with value receivers; pointer receivers reserved for commands; slices.Clone/maps.Clone
implementation_notes: Go's local idiom encodes the split in the receiver: a value receiver works on a copy and cannot change the caller's struct, while mutation requires a pointer receiver - the Go Code Review Comments state it as 'if the method needs to mutate the receiver, the receiver must be a pointer'. Strings are immutable, but slices and maps are shared references, so a value receiver copies only the header: returning a modified copy means appending to a cloned slice (slices.Clone/maps.Clone, Go 1.21+) or building a fresh one. const declares compile-time scalars only, so rates and limits can be constants but slices, maps and structs cannot; keep pointer receivers where mutation is the point or the struct is large, and name those methods as commands.
pitfalls: A value receiver still shares the backing array of a slice or map member: writing an element is visible to the caller even though the receiver was copied (appending is not).

Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex or other synchronising field is a bug - the standard library says such values must not be copied after first use, and go vet flags it; use pointer receivers throughout such a type.
A method that returns a slice hands out its internal storage; return slices.Clone(...) when the caller must not be able to mutate the original.
